title: Acid–base theories
examples: What is the difference between an acid according to Arrhenius and one according to Brønsted-Lowry?
Can you give me an example of a Lewis acid that is not a metal ion?
How do I determine the conjugate acid and base pair in a reaction?

explain.say: Today we are learning about different theories to define acids and bases.

items: Arrhenius: Acids produce H+ in water.
Lewis: Acids accept an electron pair.

explain.say: The Arrhenius theory states that acids are substances that increase hydrogen ions in water.
The Brønsted-Lowry theory says an acid is a proton donor, which is H+.
The Lewis theory is the broadest; acids are defined as electron pair acceptors.
Consider the reaction between ammonia and water to see the pairs.
In this example, water acts as the acid because it donates a proton.

draw.text: Water donates H+ to form OH-

faq.q: Do all acids produce hydrogen ions in water?
faq.a: No, the Lewis definition is broader than just water reactions. It focuses on electron pairs.
asks: Is H+ always involved in acid definitions?
What if the reaction does not happen in water?

faq.q: How do I know if something is a Lewis acid?
faq.a: You look for an atom that has an empty orbital and can accept a pair of electrons. Boron trifluoride is a good example.
asks: Does having an empty orbital mean it is an acid?
Is accepting electrons the only way to be a Lewis acid?

faq.a: A conjugate pair are two species that differ only by the gain or loss of a proton, H+. They are acid-base partners.
asks: How do I find the conjugate base from an acid?
If an acid loses a proton, what is the resulting species?

faq.q: Can a substance be both an acid and a base?
faq.a: Yes, these are called amphoteric substances. Water is the classic example of this behavior.
asks: Are there any substances that act as both?
Does the reaction conditions determine if it is an acid or base?

faq.q: Is the Arrhenius theory still useful today?
faq.a: It is useful for simple, aqueous solutions, but the Brønsted-Lowry and Lewis theories are more general.
asks: Does Arrhenius theory cover all acids?
When should I use the Lewis theory instead?

facts: Arrhenius theory is limited to aqueous solutions.
Brønsted-Lowry acidity involves the transfer of a proton, H+.
Lewis acids are defined by their ability to accept an electron pair.
A conjugate pair differs by exactly one proton.

quiz.say: Which theory defines an acid as a proton donor?
quiz.why: This definition specifically describes the donation of a proton, which is the core concept of Brønsted-Lowry theory.

wrong.0: The Lewis theory focuses on electron pairs, not just protons.
wrong.1: These theories describe different aspects of acidity, not the proton donation itself.
wrong.3: This theory only considers the production of H+ in water, which is too specific.

quiz.say: If $\text{BF}3$ reacts with $\text{NH}3$, what role does $\text{BF}3$ play?
quiz.why: Boron in $\text{BF}3$ has an empty p-orbital and accepts the lone pair from ammonia, making it a Lewis acid.

wrong.1: It does not donate a proton, so it does not fit the Brønsted-Lowry definition.
wrong.2: It is accepting electrons, not donating them.
wrong.3: This theory requires the presence of water to define acidity.

quiz.say: In the reaction $\text{HCO}3^- \rightleftharpoons ext{H}^+ + ext{CO}3^{2-}$, what is the conjugate base of $\text{H}2 ext{CO}3$?
quiz.why: The conjugate base is formed when the acid ($ ext{H}2 ext{CO}3$) loses a proton ($ ext{H}^+$).

wrong.0: The conjugate base must be a species that results after losing a proton.
wrong.2: This is the conjugate base of $ ext{HCO}3^-$, not the other way around.
wrong.3: This molecule is not directly involved in the proton transfer shown.
